Overall Assessment

This manuscript addresses a timely and relevant question: whether large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT-4.0, can generate scientific titles that are perceived as more accurate, appealing, and preferable than human-written titles. The study is clearly written, methodologically transparent, and thoughtfully situated within the emerging literature on AI-assisted academic writing. The use of blinded human raters, articles published before the advent of generative AI, and multiple statistical approaches are notable strengths.

At the same time, several aspects of the design, interpretation, and framing would benefit from clarification or refinement. Most of these do not undermine the core findings but would strengthen the rigor, scope, and interpretability of the study. With revisions, this work has strong potential to make a meaningful contribution to the literature on AI in scientific communication.

1. Conceptualization of “Perceived Accuracy”

Strength:

The authors appropriately focus on reader-centered evaluation rather than automated metrics, which is a valuable contribution compared to prior studies.

Suggestion:

The construct of “perceived accuracy” would benefit from clearer conceptual framing. Because raters evaluated titles based only on the abstract (and were not domain experts for each topic), the measure appears to capture 
                perceived alignment between title and abstract rather than factual or methodological accuracy of the study itself. 
                The authors may consider clarifying this distinction throughout the manuscript.
                    Rephrasing some claims to emphasize 
                            perceived representativeness or 
                            abstract–title alignment would improve conceptual precision.

2. Use of Articles from the Year 2000

Strength:

Selecting pre-AI articles is an elegant design choice that convincingly eliminates the possibility of AI-assisted human titles.

Suggestion:

At the same time, this introduces a potential temporal effect: writing conventions, stylistic norms, and reader expectations may have changed over 25 years. AI-generated titles, trained on modern scientific language, may naturally align better with contemporary preferences.

4. Interpretation of “Preference” as Title Quality

Strength:

Using overall preference as an outcome is intuitive and directly relevant to how readers interact with scientific articles.

Suggestion:

Preference, appeal, and perceived accuracy are inherently subjective constructs and may not fully capture other dimensions of title quality, such as precision, cautiousness of claims, or indexing suitability. 
                The Discussion could benefit from acknowledging that higher appeal does not always equate to higher epistemic rigor.
                    A brief reflection on possible trade-offs (e.g., rhetorical optimization versus conservative scientific framing) would enrich the interpretive depth.

5. Modeling of Ordinal Data

Strength:

The authors appropriately use non-parametric tests for paired comparisons and apply multilevel models to account for clustering by rater.

Suggestion:

The use of negative binomial regression for 0–10 ordinal ratings could be more fully justified, as these scores are not count data in the conventional sense.

6. Inter-Rater Agreement

Strength:

Reporting both percent agreement and Gwet’s AC with weighted coefficients is commendable and demonstrates careful attention to reliability.

Given that agreement was in the moderate-to-substantial range, the manuscript might briefly note that judgments of title quality remain partly subjective.

7. Ethics and Responsible Use of AI

Strength:

The manuscript commendably addresses ethical issues such as transparency, authorship, and the potential homogenization of scientific writing.

Suggestion:

This section could be modestly expanded to engage more directly with current debates in scholarly publishing, such as: 
                whether AI-assisted title generation constitutes authorship, editing, or technical assistance;
                    how journals might operationalize disclosure of AI use. This would strengthen the practical relevance of the study.

8. Literature balance:

The Introduction provides a strong overview of recent studies on AI-assisted scientific writing, which effectively situates the work within the current technological discourse. To further strengthen the theoretical grounding, the authors may consider incorporating additional literature on scientific title construction, rhetorical framing, and scientometrics from information science and bibliometrics. Integrating these perspectives could enrich the conceptual framework and more firmly anchor the s

The study addresses a timely question and uses an appropriate blinded paired-title design: 50 abstracts from 10 high-impact general internal medicine journals (year 2000) were retitled with GPT-4.0, and 21 researchers rated each human vs AI title for accuracy and appeal (0–10) and chose an overall preference. The work is generally clear, technically sound, and supported by open underlying/extended data. However, two points must be fixed for scientific soundness: (1) correct the inconsistency in the reported rating scale (0–10 vs 1–10) and confirm the coding used in all analyses; and (2) reconsider modeling bounded ordinal ratings with negative binomial regression. An ordinal mixed-effects model (or a clearly justified alternative with sensitivity analyses) would better match the outcome type and should explicitly account for repeated measures across raters and articles. Additional improvements: specify the random article-selection procedure (sampling frame, method/seed) and standardize formatting (e.g., capitalization) for both title types to avoid confounding.

Dear Editor and Authors,

Thank you for inviting me to review this body of work.

The article reports on the adaptation and pilot validation of the Interprofessional Socialization and Valuing Scale (ISVS-24) for use in multiplayer virtual reality (MPVR)–based interprofessional education where the authors translated the original ISVS-24 into Indonesian, conducted expert content validation, and administered a reduced 21-item version to 72 participants who are health professionals following participation in a VR simulation scenario.

The overall study design is appropriate at a pilot and exploratory level. The phased approach to translation the instrument in order to do the content validation, and preliminary psychometric testing is well considered, particularly in a novel educational context such as MPVR based simulations. The ethical procedures are clearly documented, and the authors appropriately situate their work within the growing literature on VR-based IPE.

However, the work is not fully technically sound as a validation study and it would appear to be better interpreted as a feasibility study or a form of preliminary exploration rather than a robust validation. For instance, the methods are really well explained, and are conceptually sound, and the study can be replicated. I found that this was a strength of this body of work, and the authors made the datasets available. However, some aspects of the translation process are insufficiently detailed, particularly which items require substantive rewording or contextual adaptation for VR, as well as for your context. The manuscript does not report what was extracted and why, what were, the commonalities etc. This would be important for others who may want to repeat this study for their own context. This is easily remedied as the authors can include the items and the justification for their choices more clearly.

​​​​​​The findings do justify claims regarding the feasibility, contextual relevance, and internal consistency of the adapted instrument in an MPVR setting. However, conclusions may come across as being overstated given the limitations in construct validation, sample size, and analytic approach.

It would also be interesting to understand what the IPE simulation scenario was in order to understand which of the IPE competencies were being enacted. It is often useful for context.

​​​​​​Overall, this manuscript addresses an important and emerging area in HPE and particularly IPE. This work has several strengths, particularly in relevance, transparency, and feasibility testing. However the article requires clearer positioning as a pilot study, more cautious interpretation of validity claims, and substantially improved reporting and justification of psychometric analyses, especially factor analysis.

Thank you for the opportunity to review this manuscript. I appreciate the authors’ efforts in adapting and validating the ISVS-24 instrument for use in a Multiplayer Virtual Reality (MPVR)–based interprofessional education setting. This topic is timely and highly relevant, given the increasing adoption of immersive VR in health professions education and the lack of validated instruments specifically tailored for VR-based interprofessional learning. This study therefore has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to the field.

That said, several aspects of the manuscript require clarification and further refinement to enhance its methodological rigor and interpretability: 
                Clarity and depth of methodological reporting
                        The translation and back-translation procedures are described at a general level. The manuscript would benefit from specifying which items required significant modification or discussion during the adaptation process, as this information is important to support content validity. Additionally, the expert review process involved only anesthesiology specialists, whereas interprofessional instruments ideally require input from experts representing multiple professions. This limitation should be clearly acknowledged in the Discussion section rather than integrated into the Methods.
                    Sample size justification for factor analysis
                        The sample size (N=72) is relatively small for conducting a stable exploratory factor analysis. Many methodological guidelines recommend a minimum of 5–10 participants per item or at least 100–200 participants for reliable factor extraction. A clear justification referencing the psychometric literature is needed to support the adequacy of the current sample.
                    Clarification of factor-analytic approach (PCA vs EFA)
                        Although the manuscript states that an Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) was conducted, the analytical procedures described—specifically the use of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) as the extraction method—do not align with the requirements of a true EFA. PCA is a data-reduction technique that does not model latent constructs. The authors should clarify whether their intention was to conduct a genuine EFA, and if so, justify the use of PCA or consider reanalyzing the data using appropriate factor-extraction methods such as Principal Axis Factoring (PAF) or Maximum Likelihood (ML). Clear reporting of communalities, factor loadings, rotation methods, and rationale for factor retention (e.g., scree plot, parallel analysis) is also needed.
                    Manuscript structure and placement of information
                        Several statements about study limitations appear within the Methods and Results sections. These should be relocated to the Discussion section to improve structural coherence and to distinguish descriptive procedures from interpretive commentary.
                    Strengthening the Discussion through comparison with prior ISVS validations
                        The Discussion section would benefit from a deeper comparison with ISVS validation studies from other countries or educational contexts. Highlighting similarities or differences in item performance, factor structures, and reliability indices would help situate the findings within the broader literature. Overall, this manuscript addresses an important and emerging area in health professions education. With clearer methodological reporting, appropriate factor-analytic procedures, and a more structured presentation of findings, the study has the potential to make a valuable contribution to the development of assessment tools for VR-based interprofessional education.

The authors are not aware that OHRQoL measured by OHIP does not have 7 dimensions. OHRQoL has four dimensions (John MT, 2020 [Ref-1]).

The authors are not aware of the recent scoring recommendations for OHIP (John MT., 2022 [Ref-2]).

Is the study design appropriate and is the work technically sound? – No

The authors performed a cross-sectional study when a longitudinal study would have been necessary to answer the research question.

Are sufficient details of methods and analysis provided to allow replication by others? – No

The central study outcome is oral health-related quality of life measured by OHIP-14.  The authors provided the following information: “Regarding the instruments, the Quality of Life (QoL) Questionnaire was used, originally designed by Slade and Spencer in 1994, adapted by Espinoza in 2017, and updated and validated in 2024 by Cruzado, Alvarado, and Lora. Loza. This questionnaire includes 14 items organized into 7 dimensions (Functional limitation, Physical pain, Psychological discomfort, Physical disabilities, Psychological disabilities, Social disability, and Disability), with 2 items per dimension. A 5-point Likert scale was applied (0 = never, 4 = very frequently), the results of which were classified into three categories: excellent (0-2 points), average (3-9 points), and poor quality of life (10 points or more).”

The authors provided in the reference list a reference to Slade and Spencer and to Espinoza; however, a reference to “updated and validated in 2024 by Cruzado, Alvarado, and Lora. Loza” is missing. Therefore, it is not clear what was measured, especially, because the authors use an item response scale ranging from “never” to “very frequently,” which is not OHIP’s original response format.

If applicable, is the statistical analysis and its interpretation appropriate? – No

For many results, e.g., “significant association between quality of life and oral health perception (Rho=0.391, p<0.05)”, the authors only provided point estimates. Confidence intervals around point estimates describe the uncertainty around the results. In this study with N=72, this uncertainty is substantial. Calculating a confidence interval according to 
                https://www.statskingdom.com/correlation-confidence-interval-calculator.html reveals that correlations as small as 0.18 and as large as 0.57 are compatible with the study. While the observed correlation of 0.391 is statistically significant, i.e., it can be differentiated from 0, the observed “medium” size correlation could be “small” or “large” when the study would be repeated, indicating that not much can be learned from the study.

Are the conclusions drawn adequately supported by the results? – No

The authors concluded “The link between quality of life and the perception of oral health in hospital staff emphasizes the need to implement comprehensive strategies that optimize their well-being and work performance, contributing significantly to improving hospital services.”

First, the authors make a statement about quality of life. However, quality of life (a construct that entails environment, safety, freedom etc.) was not measured. ORAL HEALTH-RELATED quality of life was measured.

Second, the magnitude of the link between oral health-related quality of life and perception of oral health is not clear. It could be small, i.e., not clinically relevant.

Third, “the need to implement comprehensive strategies” is not supported by the cross-sectional study design.
